2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the appellants as pre-emptors filed Miscellaneous (pre-emption) Case No. 6 of 1998 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Thana Borura, District-Comilla against Abdul Hamid, the predecessor-in-interest of the pre-emptee-respondent Nos. 1-8 herein praying for pre-emption of the case land measuring .32 acre out of .70 acre, as fully described in the schedule to the application for pre-emption. The pre-emptors stated, inter alia, that the case land measuring .32 acre along with the remaining land measuring .38 acre of the disputed Dag Nos. 189-193 and khatian No.208 originally belonged to Sridam Chandra Mazumder and his name was correctly recorded in the Khatian. After his death his only son Surya Kumar Mazumder, opposite party No. 2 (in the miscellaneous case), became the owner and, thereafter, he gifted .40 acre of land therefrom to his wife-Sagori Rani by a deed of gift dated 16.11.1991 and she thereafter sold the same to the pre-emptor No. 1 by a deed of sale dated 02.1.2003 and put him in possession. The opposite party No. 2 sold .041/2 acre of land from plot No. 168 and .28 acre of land from plot No. 185 in total .321/2 acre by a deed dated 24.1.1993. He also sold .42 acre of land from plot No. 184 to the pre-emptors by a deed dated 20.4.1993. In this way the pre-emptors became co-sharers in the disputed S.A. Khatian No.208 by purchase. The vendor-opposite party No. 2 sold the case land to the pre-emptee by a deed of sale dated 25.9.1994 without serving a notice upon the pre-emptors, who are co-sharers in the disputed jote. 

 4. Respondent Nos. 1-8, heirs of Abdul Hamid as pre-emptees contested the pre-emption case by filing written objection denying the material facts in the pre-emption petition contending, inter alia, that the matter of exchange was genuine and that the subsequent purchasers (his sons) are the necessary parties in the case, and the case cannot proceed without making them party. The opposite party No. 2 after exchanging .32 acre of land with the land of the pre-emptee again sold .32 acre of land out of the remaining .38 acre to Shahidullah and others (sons of the pre-emptee) by a deed of sale dated. 16.10.1994, and he also sold the remaining .06 acre of land to Al-Mamun, son of the pre-emptor by another deed dated 20.2.1995. During survey operation, these lands were wrongly recorded in the name of the transferee for which both of these purchasers filed objection under rule 30 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules and both of these objections were heard on the same date and the record was corrected and the pre-emptor knew of the sale from that date and not on 24.2.1998 as claimed by him. The case is, therefore, liable to be dismissed being barred by limitation. 

 8. Mr. Sharif Uddin Chaklader, learned Advocate appearing for the appellants made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. The learned Advocate further submitted that the High Court Division miserably failed to appreciate that the trial Court clearly and categorically discussed the oral evidence of both the parties to the effect that admittedly the pre-emptor is a co-sharer and the pre-emptee is a stranger in the case land and that the pre-emptee has failed to prove that the case deed is a deed of exchange and that the appellate Court agreed with the findings and decision arrived at by the trial Court, and that it is not open to the revisional court to re-open the findings of fact arrived at by the courts below. He further submitted that the High Court Division committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in not taking into consideration the fact that in its revisional jurisdiction the High Court Division cannot enter into the question of propriety or otherwise of the Courts below in relying on the evidence of the witnesses, if it is found that the Courts below duly considered and analysed the evidence adduced by the parties. He also submitted that the High Court Division committed a serious error of law in not finding that in view of the reasons stated in the judgment and order passed by the Courts below, the said Courts committed no illegality in allowing the application for pre-emption and no inference with the decisions of the Courts below is called for by the revisional Court. The learned Advocate lastly submitted that the High Court Division transgressed its jurisdiction in setting aside the judgments and orders of the Courts below based on con-current findings of fact, which amounts to assessment of evidence afresh. Credibility, trustworthiness etc. of witnesses are matters pertaining to the domain of appreciation of evidence, a special preserve of the trial Court and the option has been exercised by the Courts below in accepting the evidence of certain witnesses apparently upon satisfaction of their credibility; the revisional Court cannot interfere with the same (43 DLR(AD)79). 

 9. Mrs. Qumrunnessa, learned Advocate appearing for the respondents made sub-missions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. She also submitted that the pre-emptor has totally failed to prove his case by evidence that the deed in question is a sale deed, but the pre-emptee through evidence of OPW-2 opposite party, second party to the deed, Opposite Party No. 3 Scribe of the deed, OPW-4 Surveyor who measured the land covered by the exchange deed, OPW-5 contiguous land holder of land under exchange deed, has substantially proved the deed in question to be an exchange deed and the findings of the trial Court as well as appellate Court are based on non-consideration of material evidence, and as such the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute reversing the judgment of the courts below. She further submitted that the deed in question contains the statement that it is a deed of exchange, the trial Court as well as the appellate Court committed error in law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice going beyond the recitals of the deed itself holding that it was a deed of sale and not of exchange, Wand as such the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute reversing the judgments of the lower Courts. She submitted that the deed in question is one for an out and out exchange and the same was accordingly prepared, executed and registered and was acted upon. In a preemption proceeding. only the recitals of the deed of transfer is the evidence to find the nature and kind of the transfer, and consideration of the surrounding facts and circumstances is not permissible in a preemption proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. She submitted that section 91 of the Evidence Act provides that oral evidence is inadmissible for the purpose of construing terms of a document and in the instant case the document itself4 is a deed of exchange and as such no oral evidence can nullify the character and status of the deed of exchange. The High Court Division having considered the relevant provision of law rightly made the Rule absolute. She lastly submitted that a deed of exchange can never be treated as an out and out sale deed in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act without a suit for declaration to that effect in a proper Court. 

 11. The case is one of pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The trial Court allowed the application mainly on the ground that the transaction of exchange as claimed by the vendor and the vendee (pre-emptee) was not believed to be a genuine exchange, rather the document disclosed the value of the land as Tk.4000/-, which gave the semblance of a sale. The trial Court took into consideration the fact that within 20 days of the exchange, the land which was received by the vendor (opposite party No.2) was returned by way of sale to the sons of the pre-emptee. Moreover, the trial Court took into account the fact that opposite party No.1 Abdul Hamid was not able to prove his ownership of land in plot No.264 and, therefore, he was not in a position to exchange land from that plot with the case land. The trial Court concluded that the deed in question was not an exchange deed.
